promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is a pathogen?
options: A disease-causing organism
A white blood cell that makes antibodies
A protein that binds to antigens
A chemical barrier in the stomach
questions.explain: A pathogen is defined as a disease-causing organism, such as certain bacteria, viruses or fungi.

questions.q: What is a transmissible disease?
options: A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another
A disease caused only by the body's own cells
A disease that cannot be caught from other people
An inherited disorder passed on through genes
questions.explain: A transmissible disease is one in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of indirect transmission of a pathogen?
options: Drinking water contaminated with a pathogen
Touching an infected person's skin directly
Inheriting a condition from a parent
Producing antibodies after an infection
questions.explain: Indirect transmission occurs via contaminated food, water, surfaces or air, rather than by direct contact with an infected host.

questions.q: Why can droplets released when a person sneezes spread disease?
options: They can carry pathogens through the air to be breathed in by others
They contain antibodies that infect other people
They kill the white blood cells of nearby people
They provide passive immunity to those nearby
questions.explain: Airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes can carry pathogens that are then inhaled by others, spreading the disease.

questions.q: Which measure would most directly reduce the transmission of a pathogen spread through contaminated water?
options: Treating sewage and providing clean drinking water
Increasing the number of lymphocytes in the body
Giving people passive immunity at birth
Encouraging people to produce more antibodies
questions.explain: Proper sewage treatment and a clean water supply prevent water-borne pathogens from reaching new hosts.

questions.q: Which of these is a mechanical barrier that defends the body against pathogens?
options: The skin
Stomach acid
Antibodies
Mucus enzymes
questions.explain: The skin is a mechanical barrier that physically prevents pathogens from entering the body.

questions.q: How does stomach acid act as a chemical defence against pathogens?
options: It kills many pathogens in swallowed food and drink
It engulfs pathogens by phagocytosis
It produces antibodies against pathogens
It forms a physical barrier over the skin
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is a chemical barrier that kills many pathogens taken in with food and drink.

questions.q: What is the role of phagocytes in defending the body?
options: They engulf and digest pathogens
They produce antibodies specific to each pathogen
They form mucus in the airways
They provide passive immunity to babies
questions.explain: Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis.

questions.q: How does mucus in the nose and airways help protect against disease?
options: It traps pathogens so they can be removed
It produces antibodies against pathogens
It kills pathogens using stomach acid
It provides long-term active immunity
questions.explain: Mucus traps pathogens and dust, helping prevent them from reaching the lungs so they can be removed.

questions.q: Which type of white blood cell produces antibodies?
options: Lymphocytes
Phagocytes
Red blood cells
Platelets
questions.explain: Lymphocytes are the white blood cells that produce antibodies against specific antigens.

questions.q: What is an antibody?
options: A protein that binds to a specific antigen
A toxin released by a pathogen
A type of pathogen that causes disease
A mechanical barrier on the skin
questions.explain: An antibody is a protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen, leading to the pathogen's destruction.

questions.q: Why does each type of pathogen require a specific antibody?
options: Each pathogen has specific antigens with a particular shape
Each pathogen releases the same toxin
Antibodies are made by phagocytes at random
All antibodies have an identical binding site
questions.explain: Antibodies have a complementary shape to particular antigens, so a specific antibody is needed for each pathogen's antigens.

questions.q: What is active immunity?
options: Defence against a pathogen by antibody production in the body after an antigen enters
Short-term protection gained by receiving ready-made antibodies
Protection provided only by mechanical barriers such as skin
Immunity that never involves memory cells
questions.explain: Active immunity is gained when an antigen enters the body and the person's own lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory cells.

questions.q: How does a vaccine produce immunity to a disease?
options: Weakened pathogens or antigens trigger lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells
It supplies ready-made antibodies that last a lifetime
It kills all pathogens already present in the blood
It strengthens the skin as a mechanical barrier
questions.explain: A vaccine contains weakened or inactivated pathogens (or their antigens) that stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells.

questions.q: Why does a person usually respond faster to a pathogen the second time they are infected?
options: Memory cells produce antibodies more quickly and in greater quantity
The skin becomes a stronger mechanical barrier
The pathogen loses all of its antigens
Passive immunity is transferred from the mother
questions.explain: Memory cells produced during the first response allow a faster, larger antibody response on re-infection.

questions.q: How do antibodies help destroy pathogens once they have bound to antigens?
options: They can cause pathogens to clump together, aiding their destruction
They form the skin as a barrier
They digest food in the stomach
They replace lost red blood cells
questions.explain: Antibodies can cause pathogens to clump together (agglutinate) and mark them for engulfing by phagocytes.

questions.q: What is passive immunity?
options: Short-term defence provided by antibodies from another individual
Long-term immunity produced by the body's own lymphocytes
Immunity gained only through vaccination
Protection provided by stomach acid
questions.explain: Passive immunity is short-term protection from antibodies acquired from another individual, such as across the placenta or in breast milk.

questions.q: Which is an example of how a baby can gain passive immunity?
options: Receiving antibodies through its mother's breast milk
Producing its own antibodies after a vaccination
Making memory cells after an infection
Developing a thicker layer of skin
questions.explain: Antibodies passed to a baby in breast milk (or across the placenta) give the baby short-term passive immunity.

questions.q: Why is passive immunity only short-lived?
options: No memory cells are made, so no new antibodies are produced
The pathogen changes its antigens too quickly
The skin barrier weakens over time
Too many antibodies are produced by lymphocytes
questions.explain: In passive immunity the antibodies are received ready-made and no memory cells are produced, so protection is lost as the antibodies break down.

questions.q: A newborn baby is protected against measles for a few weeks because of antibodies received from its mother, but this protection soon fades. Which type of immunity is this?
options: Passive immunity
Active immunity from vaccination
Active immunity from infection
Immunity from a mechanical barrier
questions.explain: The baby received ready-made antibodies from the mother without making memory cells, so this is short-lived passive immunity.

questions.q: A student catches chickenpox, recovers, and never gets it again despite later exposure. Which type of immunity best explains this?
options: Active immunity gained from infection
Passive immunity from breast milk
Immunity provided by stomach acid
Passive immunity from the placenta
questions.explain: After infection the student's own lymphocytes made antibodies and memory cells, giving long-lasting active immunity.

questions.q: In an area with poor sanitation, many people fall ill after drinking from the same well. What is the most likely route of transmission?
options: Indirect transmission through contaminated water
Direct transmission through skin contact
Passive immunity from the mother
Inheritance of the disease from parents
questions.explain: A shared, contaminated water source spreading a pathogen is an example of indirect transmission through water.

questions.q: A government vaccinates a large proportion of the population against a disease. Why does this help protect even unvaccinated people?
options: Fewer people can catch and pass on the pathogen, reducing its spread
Vaccinated people give passive immunity to others by touch
The vaccine removes all pathogens from the environment
The skin of vaccinated people blocks the pathogen for everyone
questions.explain: Widespread vaccination lowers the number of people who can be infected and transmit the pathogen, slowing its spread through the population.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610) syllabus; Diseases & Immunity
